options.text: Consciousness is non-physical and therefore inexplicable
options.why_wrong: McGinn holds there is a natural, physical answer.
That is the Type-C hope McGinn rejects for human minds.

options.text: There is a natural solution, but human minds are cognitively closed to it

questions.explanation: McGinn compares us to a dog that cannot grasp arithmetic: the property linking brain to consciousness exists but is beyond our concept-forming capacities. Critics call the view untestable and premature.

sources.citation: McGinn, C. (1989). Can we solve the mind-body problem? Mind 98(391), 349-366.

questions.prompt: How does neutral monism differ from idealism?

options.text: Idealism grounds the physical in the mental; neutral monism grounds both in something neither mental nor physical
Idealism grounds the mental in the physical; neutral monism denies either exists
options.why_wrong: Idealism makes the mental basic, not the physical.

options.text: They are two names for the same view
options.why_wrong: They differ in what is fundamental.

options.text: Neutral monism is a form of substance dualism
options.why_wrong: It is a monism, so not dualist.

questions.explanation: Idealists such as Berkeley make the mental fundamental; neutral monists such as Russell and James make a more basic neutral reality fundamental, with mind and matter as two ways of organising it. Both must explain why the physical world is so objective and law-governed.

sources.citation: Berkeley, G. (1710). A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge. Dublin: Jeremy Pepyat.
Russell, B. (1921). The Analysis of Mind. London: George Allen and Unwin.
